examples: She always takes the bus to work.
The store is always busy on Saturdays.
Do you always eat lunch at your desk?
I'll always remember that trip.
I've always wanted to see the Grand Canyon.
No matter what happens, we'll always be friends.
He's always borrowing money and never paying it back.
Why are you always interrupting me?
If you miss the bus, you can always call a cab.
We can always try again tomorrow.
Too expensive? Well, you could always rent one.

senses.head: At all times; on every occasion
examples: She always takes the bus to work.
The store is always busy on Saturdays.
Do you always eat lunch at your desk?

senses.head: For all time, as far back as one remembers or into the future
examples: I'll always remember that trip.
I've always wanted to see the Grand Canyon.
No matter what happens, we'll always be friends.

senses.head: Again and again, in an annoying way — with a continuous tense
examples: He's always borrowing money and never paying it back.
Why are you always interrupting me?

senses.head: As a possible choice if nothing else works — usually with can or could
examples: If you miss the bus, you can always call a cab.
We can always try again tomorrow.
Too expensive? Well, you could always rent one.

entries.type: frequency — the top of the scale; also duration (I'll always remember)
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; front only in commands (Always lock the door)
entries.form: old compound of all + way with adverbial -s
entries.contrast: Position: I always walk to work, not I walk always to work; after be it follows the verb: She is always late. Not always is 'не всегда' (He's not always right); always not is wrong — say never. With a continuous tense it turns into a complaint: He's always complaining (вечно жалуется), not a neutral habit. 'Всегда' reaching up to now takes the present perfect: I've always lived here, not I always live here since childhood.

entries.meaning: In most cases; as a rule. ---
examples: I usually get up at seven.
Traffic is usually light on Sundays.
Usually, the meeting ends by noon.
entries.type: frequency — high on the scale, just below always
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; also front or end for emphasis
entries.contrast: A habit that has stopped is used to, not usually + past: I used to walk to school (раньше ходил), while I usually walked only describes the typical case back then. 'Как обычно' is as usual, never as usually. Do not mix it up with be used to (привыкнуть): I'm used to the noise.

examples: I normally walk to work, but it's raining today.
The drive normally takes about an hour.
Normally, we'd be closed by now.
The patient is breathing normally again.
Just act normally and nobody will notice.
Is the engine running normally now?

senses.head: Usually; under ordinary conditions
examples: I normally walk to work, but it's raining today.
The drive normally takes about an hour.
Normally, we'd be closed by now.

senses.head: In a normal way; as expected, with nothing wrong
examples: The patient is breathing normally again.
Just act normally and nobody will notice.
Is the engine running normally now?

entries.position: mid — also front in the sense 'usually'; end in the sense 'in a normal way'
entries.comparison: not gradable — in the sense 'usually'; more normally is possible in the sense 'in a normal way'
entries.contrast: Russian нормально meaning 'fine, OK' is not normally: How are you? — Fine (or OK), not Normally; Everything's fine, not Everything is normally. In American English normally means 'обычно' far more often than 'нормально'.

examples: I generally skip breakfast.
Flights are generally cheaper on Tuesdays.
The weather here is generally mild in the fall.
It is generally accepted that smoking causes cancer.
The new mayor is generally well liked.
The drug is not yet generally available.
Generally speaking, the reviews were positive.
She talked about the economy generally, not about any one company.

senses.head: Usually; in most cases
examples: I generally skip breakfast.
Flights are generally cheaper on Tuesdays.
The weather here is generally mild in the fall.

senses.head: By most people; widely
examples: It is generally accepted that smoking causes cancer.
The new mayor is generally well liked.
The drug is not yet generally available.

senses.head: In broad terms, without going into details
examples: Generally speaking, the reviews were positive.
She talked about the economy generally, not about any one company.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be; also front, especially in generally speaking
entries.comparison: not gradable — more generally means 'in broader terms'
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives, participles and whole clauses
entries.contrast: Generally is 'обычно' or 'в целом', not the emphatic 'вообще' of negatives and questions: Я вообще не пью is I don't drink at all; А ты вообще кто? is Who are you, anyway? The set phrase generally speaking is 'вообще говоря'.

examples: He travels frequently for work.
Check the list of frequently asked questions first.
Buses run more frequently during rush hour.
entries.contrast: Frequently is more formal than often; the everyday question is How often…?, not How frequently…? It sits comfortably at the end: It happens frequently.

examples: We often eat dinner on the porch in the summer.
How often do you go to the gym?
I wish we could visit more often.
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; also end, especially with very, quite or too
entries.comparison: more/most — more often, most often; oftener is rare
entries.contrast: Position: I often go there, not I go often there; at the end it is most natural with a partner: We don't eat out very often. The t is normally silent (AW-fuhn), though AWF-tuhn is also heard. Every so often means 'время от времени' (not often), and more often than not means 'обычно'.

entries.meaning: On some occasions, but not always. ---
examples: Sometimes I just need a quiet day at home.
My sister sometimes works from home.
The subway gets really crowded sometimes.
entries.type: frequency — the middle of the scale
entries.position: any position — front, mid and end are all natural
entries.contrast: Three different words: sometimes (иногда — I sometimes work late), sometime (когда-нибудь, в какой-то момент — Let's have lunch sometime) and some time (некоторое время — It took some time).

examples: We occasionally go out for Mexican food.
I run into him at the gym occasionally.
The trail is occasionally closed after heavy rain.
entries.type: frequency — below sometimes on the scale
entries.contrast: It means 'now and then', not 'by chance': 'случайно' is by chance or accidentally. Spelled with double c and single s. It suggests fewer times than sometimes — roughly once in a while.

examples: We seldom see snow this far south.
He seldom talks about his time in the Army.
Seldom have I heard such a moving speech.
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (Seldom do we…)
entries.contrast: It is already negative, so no not: I seldom go, not I don't seldom go; the question tag is positive: He seldom calls, does he? Fronted for emphasis, it inverts: Seldom have I seen such a mess, not Seldom I have seen. In everyday American speech rarely or not often is more usual; seldom sounds formal or bookish.

examples: I rarely watch TV anymore.
She is rarely late for work.
Rarely does a rookie play this well.
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (Rarely does it…)
entries.contrast: Already negative, so no not: I rarely eat meat; the question tag is positive: She rarely complains, does she? Fronted, it inverts: Rarely does it snow here, not Rarely it snows here. Rarely if ever and hardly ever are standard; rarely ever is informal.

examples: I've never been to Alaska.
She never drinks coffee after lunch.
Never have I felt so welcome.
He never even said goodbye.
I never touched your phone, I swear.
The package never arrived.

senses.head: At no time; not once
examples: I've never been to Alaska.
She never drinks coffee after lunch.
Never have I felt so welcome.

senses.head: Not, said with emphasis — often about a single occasion
examples: He never even said goodbye.
I never touched your phone, I swear.
The package never arrived.

entries.type: frequency — the bottom of the scale; also negative
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (Never have I…) or in commands (Never give up)
entries.form: old ne 'not' + ever — negative in itself
entries.contrast: English allows one negative: I never eat meat, not I don't never eat meat (Russian никогда не doubles it). Fronted, it inverts: Never have I felt so tired. For experience use the present perfect: I've never been to Chicago. In questions use ever: Have you ever…?, not Have you never…? unless you are surprised. Informal I never took it is about one occasion and means 'I didn't take it'.

examples: Have you ever tried sushi?
Nobody ever calls the landline.
If you're ever in Denver, look us up.
This is the best pizza I've ever had.
She was the first woman ever to run the company.
Gas prices are higher than ever this summer.
He's been sad ever since his dog died.
And they lived happily ever after.
She was, as ever, the last one to leave.
Prices keep climbing to ever higher levels.
The suburbs are spreading ever farther from the city.
Boy, was she ever mad!
Did we ever have fun at that concert!
How can I ever thank you?
She opened the door ever so slightly.
He lifted the sleeping baby ever so gently.

senses.head: At any time — in questions, negatives and conditions
examples: Have you ever tried sushi?
Nobody ever calls the landline.
If you're ever in Denver, look us up.

senses.head: Of all time — after a superlative, after first or only, and in than ever
examples: This is the best pizza I've ever had.
She was the first woman ever to run the company.
Gas prices are higher than ever this summer.

senses.head: Always; all the time — in fixed phrases such as ever since, ever after and as ever
examples: He's been sad ever since his dog died.
And they lived happily ever after.
She was, as ever, the last one to leave.

senses.head: More and more — before a comparative
examples: Prices keep climbing to ever higher levels.
The suburbs are spreading ever farther from the city.

senses.head: Used for emphasis — in informal American exclamations with inversion, and after how or why in questions
examples: Boy, was she ever mad!
Did we ever have fun at that concert!
How can I ever thank you?

senses.head: Very; in the smallest or gentlest way — in ever so before an adverb or adjective
examples: She opened the door ever so slightly.
He lifted the sleeping baby ever so gently.

entries.position: mid — after the subject in questions (Have you ever…?) and after the negative word (nobody ever); after its word after a superlative (the best ever); before its word in ever higher and ever so
entries.modifies: verbs, superlatives, comparatives, so and whole clauses
entries.contrast: Not in a plain affirmative statement: 'я когда-то был в Париже' is I've been to Paris or I was once in Paris, never I have ever been to Paris. Use it in questions (Have you ever…?), negatives (nobody ever, hardly ever), conditions (if you ever…) and after superlatives (the best ever). 'Как никогда' after a comparative is than ever: I need you more than ever, not like never. Ever so (ever so slightly) is informal and more British, but common in American writing. Ever since is 'с тех пор'; forever is written as one word in American English.

examples: The museum is open daily from 9 to 5.
Take this pill twice daily with food.
The list of volunteers is growing daily.
entries.position: end — not mid (The paper comes out daily)
entries.form: -ly from day; the same form as the adjective daily
entries.contrast: The same spelling is an adjective (a daily newspaper) and a noun (a daily — ежедневная газета); only 'every day' after a verb is the adverb. Keep it at the end: We exercise daily, not We daily exercise. Also do not confuse the phrase every day (каждый день) with the adjective everyday (повседневный).

examples: The team meets weekly to review progress.
The newsletter goes out weekly.
At this job we get paid weekly.
entries.form: -ly from week; the same form as the adjective weekly
entries.contrast: Also an adjective (a weekly meeting) and a noun (a weekly — еженедельник). Biweekly is ambiguous — it can mean twice a week or every two weeks — so Americans often say every other week to be clear.

examples: Rent is due monthly, on the first.
The book club meets monthly at the library.
Interest on the account is paid monthly.
entries.form: -ly from month; the same form as the adjective monthly
entries.contrast: Also an adjective (a monthly payment) and a noun (a monthly — ежемесячный журнал). Bimonthly can mean twice a month or every two months; every other month avoids the doubt.

examples: The company reports its earnings quarterly.
Freelancers pay estimated taxes quarterly.
The board meets quarterly.
entries.form: -ly from quarter; the same form as the adjective quarterly
entries.contrast: It means every three months — a quarter of a year — not every quarter of an hour. Also an adjective (quarterly earnings) and a noun (a quarterly — ежеквартальный журнал).

examples: The festival is held annually in June.
About two million people visit the park annually.
Salaries are reviewed annually.
entries.contrast: Formal and financial; everyday speech says every year or once a year. Biannually means twice a year, biennially every two years. Spelled with double n and double l.

examples: We see the dentist twice yearly.
The membership fee is paid yearly.
The town holds the parade yearly on the Fourth of July.
entries.form: -ly from year; the same form as the adjective yearly
entries.contrast: The everyday counterpart of annually; also an adjective (a yearly checkup). The vowel is the one in year (YEER-lee), not the one in early (UR-lee).

examples: Trains leave for the city hourly.
The nurse checks his temperature hourly.
Most of the store staff are paid hourly.
Lawyers usually bill hourly.

senses.head: Once an hour; every hour
examples: Trains leave for the city hourly.
The nurse checks his temperature hourly.

senses.head: By the hour; for each hour worked
examples: Most of the store staff are paid hourly.
Lawyers usually bill hourly.

entries.form: -ly from hour; the same form as the adjective hourly
entries.contrast: The h is silent, so the adjective takes an: an hourly bus, an hourly wage. American hourly workers are paid by the hour, as opposed to salaried ones.

examples: The show runs nightly at eight.
The kitchen is open nightly until eleven.
She checks the locks nightly before bed.
entries.form: -ly from night; the same form as the adjective nightly
entries.contrast: It usually means every evening — shows and TV news run nightly — and never simply 'ночью': for that say at night (Owls hunt at night). Also an adjective (the nightly news).

examples: I've been to Chicago twice.
Brush your teeth twice a day.
The phone rang twice and then stopped.
Their house is twice as big as ours.
The repairs took twice as long as we planned.

senses.head: Two times; on two occasions
examples: I've been to Chicago twice.
Brush your teeth twice a day.
The phone rang twice and then stopped.

senses.head: Two times as much — in comparisons
examples: Their house is twice as big as ours.
The repairs took twice as long as we planned.

entries.type: frequency — definite; also degree (twice as big)
entries.position: end — before its word in twice as … as
entries.form: two + old adverbial -ce, like once; the series goes once, twice, then three times
entries.contrast: 'В два раза больше' is twice as big (as) or twice the size (of); two times bigger is heard but criticized. Frequency takes no preposition: twice a week, not twice in a week (unless you mean 'within one week'). Thrice is archaic — say three times.

examples: Could you say that again?
I failed the test, so I'll take it again in May.
Oh no, it's raining again.
It's good to be home again.
She's feeling well again after the surgery.
What was your name again?
Where are we meeting again?
Again, I want to thank everyone for coming.
Again, the problem is money, not time.
It's expensive. Then again, it'll last for years.
I might go. But then again, I might not.

senses.head: One more time; once more
examples: Could you say that again?
I failed the test, so I'll take it again in May.
Oh no, it's raining again.

senses.head: Back to an earlier place or condition
examples: It's good to be home again.
She's feeling well again after the surgery.

senses.head: Used to ask for information that you were told but have forgotten
examples: What was your name again?
Where are we meeting again?

senses.head: Used to repeat or stress a point already made
examples: Again, I want to thank everyone for coming.
Again, the problem is money, not time.

senses.head: On the other hand — in then again and but then again
examples: It's expensive. Then again, it'll last for years.
I might go. But then again, I might not.

entries.position: end — mid in formal writing; front in Again, … and Then again, …
entries.contrast: English again is neutral; Russian опять can sound annoyed, and English shows that with yet again or Not again! What's his name again? is not 'ещё раз' in the sense of doing something over — it means 'напомни, как его зовут'. 'Повторно' is again or a second time, not repeatedly (много раз). Most Americans say uh-GEN; uh-GAYN is also heard.

entries.meaning: All the time, or so often that it seems like all the time. ---
examples: The baby cried constantly the first week.
Technology is constantly changing.
He's constantly checking his phone during dinner.
entries.contrast: Constantly (постоянно, всё время) is not consistently (неизменно, стабильно): He's constantly late means he is late all the time; Her work is consistently good means it is reliably good. With a continuous tense it signals irritation: You're constantly checking your phone.

examples: She exercises regularly.
Change your passwords regularly.
I wish the buses ran more regularly out here.
The fence posts are regularly spaced, ten feet apart.
His heart is beating regularly now.
These jeans are regularly $60, now on sale for $40.
All regularly priced items are 20% off today.

senses.head: Often and as a habit, or at fixed intervals
examples: She exercises regularly.
Change your passwords regularly.
I wish the buses ran more regularly out here.

senses.head: Evenly; in an even pattern or rhythm
examples: The fence posts are regularly spaced, ten feet apart.
His heart is beating regularly now.

senses.head: At the usual price — in American stores and ads
examples: These jeans are regularly $60, now on sale for $40.
All regularly priced items are 20% off today.

entries.contrast: Regularly stresses a steady pattern, so it is not always often: I see him regularly suggests a routine (every Tuesday); I see him often just means many times. On American price tags regularly means 'at the usual price': regularly $50, now $35.

examples: I repeatedly asked him to turn the music down.
The company had been warned repeatedly.
She pressed the button repeatedly, but nothing happened.
entries.contrast: Repeatedly means many times, not one more time: I asked him again (ещё раз) vs I asked him repeatedly (много раз). Russian повторно (a second time) is again or a second time.

examples: He continually interrupts when other people are talking.
The office printer continually jams.
The city's population has grown continually since 1950.
Our software is continually being improved.

senses.head: Again and again over a period of time, often annoyingly
examples: He continually interrupts when other people are talking.
The office printer continually jams.

senses.head: Without stopping; all the time
examples: The city's population has grown continually since 1950.
Our software is continually being improved.

entries.contrast: Careful writers split the pair: continually is 'again and again, with breaks' (The phone rang continually), continuously is 'with no break at all' (The engine ran continuously for ten hours). Everyday American usage also lets continually mean 'without stopping', so choose continuously when the absence of breaks matters.

examples: It rained continuously for three days.
The machines run continuously, twenty-four hours a day.
She has lived in the same town continuously since birth.
entries.contrast: Not the same as continually: It rained continuously means it never stopped; It rained continually means it kept raining on and off.

entries.meaning: From time to time, often at more or less regular intervals. ---
examples: Check the tire pressure periodically.
The website is updated periodically.
He periodically glanced at the clock.

entries.meaning: As a normal, regular part of a procedure or of life; as a matter of course. ---
examples: Bags are routinely checked at the entrance.
Doctors routinely test newborns for hearing problems.
He routinely works sixty-hour weeks.
entries.русский: как правило, регулярно, в обычном порядке
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary
entries.contrast: Russian рутинно sounds dull and mechanical; English routinely is neutral — 'as standard practice': Newborns are routinely tested means every newborn is tested as a matter of course. It can also mean 'so often that it is no longer surprising': He routinely ignores my emails.

entries.meaning: Now and then, irregularly and with no pattern. ---
examples: Fighting continued sporadically through the night.
He attended class only sporadically.
The Wi-Fi in this hotel works sporadically at best.
entries.contrast: Not the same as periodically: sporadically stresses irregular, scattered occurrences with no pattern, while periodically suggests intervals.

examples: I wish this summer could last forever.
Once you post it online, it's there forever.
The accident changed their lives forever.
The line at the DMV took forever.
I've known her forever.
He's forever losing his glasses.
My neighbors are forever complaining about something.

senses.head: For all future time; permanently
examples: I wish this summer could last forever.
Once you post it online, it's there forever.
The accident changed their lives forever.

senses.head: For a very long time — an informal exaggeration
examples: The line at the DMV took forever.
I've known her forever.

senses.head: Constantly; all the time — with a continuous tense
examples: He's forever losing his glasses.
My neighbors are forever complaining about something.

entries.position: end — mid in be forever doing
entries.form: compound of for + ever, written as one word in American English
entries.contrast: American English writes forever as one word in every sense; for ever is British. With a continuous tense it means 'constantly' and sounds annoyed: He's forever losing his keys (вечно теряет). Take forever is informal exaggeration, not literal. For good is a common informal synonym of 'навсегда'.

examples: She briefly worked as a waitress in college.
The power went out briefly during the storm.
We stopped briefly in Memphis.
Let me explain briefly how it works.
Briefly, the answer is no.
Could you put that more briefly?

senses.head: For a short time
examples: She briefly worked as a waitress in college.
The power went out briefly during the storm.
We stopped briefly in Memphis.

senses.head: In a few words; in short
examples: Let me explain briefly how it works.
Briefly, the answer is no.
Could you put that more briefly?

entries.position: mid or end — front in Briefly, … (in short)
entries.contrast: Briefly is about length (ненадолго, кратко); shortly means 'soon' (вскоре): I'll speak briefly means the speech will be short, I'll speak shortly means it will start soon.

entries.meaning: For a period of time with no fixed end. ---
examples: The concert has been postponed indefinitely.
You can't keep living with your parents indefinitely.
The plant will stay closed indefinitely.
entries.contrast: It means 'with no end date fixed', not 'endlessly': a concert postponed indefinitely may still happen. 'Бесконечно' is endlessly or infinitely, and vague 'неопределённо' is vaguely.

examples: I was momentarily blinded by the headlights.
She paused momentarily before answering.
The doctor will be with you momentarily.
We will be landing momentarily.

senses.head: For a moment; very briefly
examples: I was momentarily blinded by the headlights.
She paused momentarily before answering.

senses.head: In a moment; very soon — mainly American
examples: The doctor will be with you momentarily.
We will be landing momentarily.

entries.contrast: US/UK split: in British English it means only 'for a moment'; in American English it very often means 'in a moment, very soon' — the flight attendant's We'll be landing momentarily. Context decides: past events and states (was momentarily confused) mean 'for a moment', future ones (will be here momentarily) mean 'soon'. American stress falls on the third syllable. False friend: Russian моментально (instantly) is instantly or right away, not momentarily.

examples: Let the dough rise overnight.
Can I stay overnight at your place?
It snowed overnight, and the roads are icy.
The video made her famous overnight.
You won't learn a language overnight.

senses.head: During the night, or for the whole night
examples: Let the dough rise overnight.
Can I stay overnight at your place?
It snowed overnight, and the roads are icy.

senses.head: Very suddenly or quickly
examples: The video made her famous overnight.
You won't learn a language overnight.

entries.русский: за ночь, на ночь; в одночасье
entries.form: compound of over + night; the same form as the adjective overnight
entries.contrast: The adverb is stressed on -night (oh-vur-NYT); the adjective before a noun (an overnight bag, an overnight success) often moves the stress to the first syllable and belongs to the adjective dictionary. Stay overnight means 'остаться на ночь', not 'не спать всю ночь' (stay up all night).

examples: The store is permanently closed.
The fire permanently damaged the old church.
Those files were permanently deleted.
He's now permanently based in our Denver office.
She's permanently employed now, not on a contract.
Is he in town permanently, or just visiting?

senses.head: For all time; in a way that will not change or cannot be undone
examples: The store is permanently closed.
The fire permanently damaged the old church.
Those files were permanently deleted.

senses.head: On a lasting basis rather than for a limited time — about where one lives or works
examples: He's now permanently based in our Denver office.
She's permanently employed now, not on a contract.
Is he in town permanently, or just visiting?

entries.contrast: Russian постоянно meaning 'all the time' is constantly or always, not permanently: He constantly calls me, not He permanently calls me. Permanently is about lasting: permanently closed (закрыто навсегда), live here permanently (жить здесь постоянно).

entries.meaning: For a limited time; not permanently.
examples: The road is temporarily closed for repairs.
I'm temporarily staying with my brother.
The website is temporarily unavailable.
entries.form: -ly from temporary, with y changed to i
entries.contrast: American stress falls on the third syllable (tem-puh-RAIR-uh-lee); British English often stresses the first. Do not confuse it with temporally (во времени, 'relating to time').
